title: Claims That Hold Up
objectives: I can name the parts of an argument: stance, premise, warrant, and evidence.
I can state a counterclaim fairly, make a concession, and rebut the objection.
I can spot a fallacy and explain why the reasoning is weak.
I can write a short argument that substantiates its claim with reasons and evidence.
rationale: Grade 7 writers must support a claim with reasoning and answer an objection, so they need a vocabulary for the parts of an argument. The unit follows an argument in order: taking a position (stance, contend), building it (premise, logic, warrant), backing it up (substantiate), testing it (fallacy), and answering the other side (counterclaim, concession, rebut). Warrant, stance, and concession each carry another meaning students already know, so the unit trains them to ask which sense a writer intends. The unit connects to the previous work on inference, rationale, validate, and verify: a claim holds up when its evidence is checked and its reasons are stated.

passage.title: Keep the Library Open Until Five
paras: My stance is simple: our school library should stay open until five o'clock on weekdays instead of closing at 3:30. I contend that an extra ninety minutes of quiet, supervised space would help students more than almost any other change the school could afford. Here is my reasoning.

The logic of my argument has three steps. My first premise is that many students have no quiet place to study at home, because they share rooms, care for younger siblings, or work. My second premise is that students who finish homework at school have more time for sleep and family. It follows that a later closing time would help the students who need it most.

A claim also needs a warrant, the reason that connects the evidence to the claim. Mine is this: a place that is quiet, open, and free removes the obstacles that keep students from working. To substantiate my claim, I surveyed sixty classmates, and forty-one said they would use the library after school if it stayed open.

Some readers will offer a counterclaim: staffing the library costs too much. I offer one concession, because the cost is real and someone must supervise. But I rebut the objection by pointing out that parent volunteers and student aides could cover the extra hours, as they already do at the book fair.

Another reader wrote that students who stay late only want to goof off. That is a fallacy, because it judges a whole group by a few imagined cases instead of by evidence. A strong argument answers the real question: will students use the time well? My survey suggests that many will, and the school board should vote yes.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word “warrant” refers to
choices: a legal paper that allows a search
a survey of sixty classmates
the reason that connects evidence to a claim
the writer's final request to the board
qs.why: The sentence defines the warrant as the reason that connects the evidence to the claim.

qs.q: Which counterclaim does the writer answer with volunteers and student aides?
choices: Students have no quiet place at home.
Too few students would use the library.
Staffing the library costs too much.
Students would rather study at home.
qs.why: The writer concedes that cost is real and then rebuts it by saying volunteers and aides could cover the hours.

qs.q: Why does the writer call the claim that late students only want to goof off a fallacy?
choices: It judges a whole group by imagined cases instead of evidence.
It was written by a teacher who disagrees.
It contradicts the results of the survey.
It is too long to be a real argument.
qs.why: The text says the claim judges a whole group by a few imagined cases, which is a mistake in reasoning.

qs.q: What is the main purpose of the survey of sixty classmates?
choices: To entertain the readers
To create a fallacy
To measure what the library costs
To support the claim with evidence from students
qs.why: The writer says the survey is meant to substantiate the claim, and forty-one of sixty said they would use the library.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Libraries cost too much to keep open.
The library should stay open later because the reasoning and evidence show it would help students.
Students should avoid doing homework at school.
Volunteers are better than paid staff.
qs.why: The writer states a stance, builds premises and a warrant, offers evidence, and answers objections to support one conclusion.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for the parts and moves of an argument: taking a stance, building premises and a warrant, backing a claim with evidence, spotting a fallacy, and answering a counterclaim with a concession and a rebuttal. They read a short student argument and write their own.

notes.va.logic.n: Logic is about the link between steps, not about whether the conclusion is right. Show a valid argument with a false premise to separate the two ideas. Do not teach formal logic notation.
notes.va.warrant.n: Warrant is the hardest word in the unit. Use the frame evidence, so, claim, and ask what must be true for the evidence to count. Students may know the police sense; show both, then say which one applies in argument.
notes.va.counterclaim.n: Teach the prefix counter- (against) and the base claim. Insist on the strongest counterclaim, not a weak one that is easy to knock down. Students often write a straw man without noticing.
notes.va.rebut.v: Rebut requires evidence. Distinguish from deny. Have students rebut a counterclaim with a fact and a reason, not just by saying it is wrong.
notes.va.concession.n: Two senses are close: admitting a point in an argument and giving up something in a deal. Show how a concession can strengthen trust. Be sure students keep the but that follows it.
notes.va.contend.v: Contend introduces a claim to be defended; the competition sense is in senses. Contrast with state and claim. Students may overuse it, so ask them to pair it with evidence.
notes.va.stance.n: A stance is a position, not a feeling. Contrast with the athletic sense. Ask students to state a stance in one sentence with no hedging, then add hedges to see the difference.
notes.va.fallacy.n: Teach two or three named fallacies simply (hasty generalization, bandwagon, attacking the person), not a long list. Emphasize that a fallacy is a flaw in reasoning, not a lie.
notes.va.premise.n: A premise is a starting statement that the argument takes as true. Contrast with conclusion. Check that students can spot a false or missing premise.
notes.va.substantiate.v: Substantiate means provide evidence, not repeat. Use a claim and ask what a skeptical reader would want to see. It pairs naturally with verify from the research unit.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: “The writer's stance is that the library should stay open until five. One premise is that many students have no quiet place at home. The warrant is that a quiet, open place removes the obstacles to working. The counterclaim is that staffing costs too much, so the writer makes a concession and then rebuts it with volunteers.”
